detail.title: Reading a Decision Tree
detail.description: Create a decision tree using the college dataset to predict whether a college is private or not, plot it, and answer: (1) without other information, would you predict a new college to be private? (2) On which variable did the tree split? (3) If f_undergrad is at least 2995, public or private? (4) From the leaves: how many public predictions, private predictions and total correct predictions? (5) Interpret with STAR.
detail.understand: The questions mirror the in-chapter TiY on penguins (Figure 8.11), which is a single-split tree, and question 3 names one threshold, so the intended tree has max depth 1. Each node shows the class counts (alphabetical: No, Yes); the predicted label is the majority. The tree chooses the split that most reduces impurity (Gini).

questions.prompt: Without knowing anything else about a new college, would you predict it to be private?
On which variable did the decision tree create a split?
If a college has f_undergrad of at least 2995, would you predict public or private?
From the leaves: how many public predictions, how many private predictions, and how many total correct predictions?
Interpret the tree using the STAR Framework.

detail.interpretation: A one-question rule on college size already classifies ~86% of training colleges correctly. It is highly interpretable but it is evaluated on the same data it learned from, so it is an optimistic estimate.
common_mistakes: Reading the counts in the wrong order: they are alphabetical (No, Yes).
Counting all observations in a leaf as correct — only the majority class in each leaf is correct.
detail.python_code:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

college = pd.read_csv("college.csv")            # DS4A Ch_8 data
X = college.drop(columns="private")             # all 17 numeric variables
y = college["private"]                          # Yes / No

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=1234).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns), show_weights=True))
# |--- f_undergrad <= 2995.00  -> weights [No=41, Yes=495] class Yes
# |--- f_undergrad >  2995.00  -> weights [No=171, Yes=70] class No

answers.explanation: The root node holds all 777 colleges: {'No': 212, 'Yes': 565}. With no other information we predict the majority class, 'Yes'.
The single split chosen by the algorithm is 'Is f_undergrad <= 2995?' — the variable whose split reduced Gini impurity the most (0.3968 → 0.2253).

Colleges with f_undergrad > 2995 go to the right leaf, which contains {'No': 171, 'Yes': 70} → majority 'No' (private = No means public). sklearn prints the threshold as 2995.0; R's rpart prints the same split as 'f_undergrad >= 2995'.
Left leaf predicts Yes for 536 colleges (495 correct); right leaf predicts No for 241 (171 correct). Total correct = 666 of 777 (training accuracy 0.8571).

answer.Scope: 777 US colleges (observational units); 17 numeric variables such as f_undergrad (full-time undergraduates); response `private` (Yes/No). Source: DS4A dataset (ISLR College, US News 1995).
answer.Track: Can a college's characteristics predict whether it is private, and which single variable separates private from public best?
answer.Articulate: The tree's first and only split is on f_undergrad at 2995. Smaller colleges (≤ 2995 full-time undergraduates) are predicted private, larger ones public. This rule is correct for 666 of 777 colleges (85.7%) in the data it was trained on.
answer.Respond: Evaluate on held-out test data (training accuracy is optimistic), try deeper trees and compare, and consider other variables such as out-of-state tuition.

answers.explanation: STAR = Scope the data's context, Track the question, Articulate the results, Respond with next steps (DS4A preface).
